newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-RBA cuts Australia rates.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-RBA cuts Australia rates.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia cut its official cash rate by 0.5 percentage points to 6.5 percent Wednesday in a widely anticipated move.
The following is a selection of economists' early reactions to the move.
NIGEL STAPLEDON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANKING CORP:
"It was easy to make a case for a cut in interest rates. Clearly, the economy is weak. We've had a tough budget, confidence is down. This easing will do something to reverse that."
KAREN PRINGLE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, FINANCIAL MARKETS, ANZ BANKING GROUP:

"I think it's enough for the time being. I think it allows them (the Reserve Bank) to sit back and wait and see how the economy is performing, and if they need to cut again they can do that in the new year...I think the outlook for growth would need to deteriorate quite a bit more from here for them to have done a larger than 50 basis point move. It's better for them to have scope up their sleeve to move again if need be."
ROB HENDERSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DRESDNER INTERNATIONAL:

"It is very much as I expected would be the case, that they've cut half a percentage point. My view is that they haven't actually said unless wages come down that rates might have to go up again. My view will be that the market will tend to build in another half a percent cut in cash rates either at the December meeting or in March. This suggests there won't be any further movements in rates for some time."
TIM PFITZNER, TREASURY ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"Certainly it's not ruling out the chance of another rate cut, if we continue to see slow wages growth, good underlying inflation towards the low end of the two to three percent (target) band, and soft labour market....I think they (the Reserve Bank) had to acknowledge that it (the economy) is a bit weak at first and they've done that. If they need to, they will follow through."
ANDREW PEASE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NOMURA RESEARCH AUSTRALIA:
"I think what the key to a further rate cut will be capex (capital expenditure) and entreprise bargaining data. Another rate cut at best is a 50-50 proposition until we see that data."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"It's a good move, a neccessary move and should ensure the economy will be OK in 1997. Any more than 0.5 point might have smacked of panic, so the size looks just right. It shows they're taking a softly, softly approach to monetary policy which should maintain its anti-inflation credibility with offshore investors. The market is starting to price in another easing, but our call at the moment is that a third cut is unlikely given there are good reasons to expect a lift in growth next year. Overall, the RBA has managed policy very well and gets a 9-1/2 out of 10 on our score card."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"The tailpiece on the statement wasn't quite as strong as I thought it might of been. Yes, there was a warning about enterprise agreements and executive pay increases, but there was no indication that they stood ready to put rates up if needed and it hasn't ruled out a further easing in this statement."

"The interesting points are that the RBA in its statement talks almost exclusively about the rate reduction being linked to an improvement in inflation and wages. It's saying inflation is the driving force. Secondly, the RBA gave greater weight to the broad AWOTE (average weekly ordinary time earnings) measure of wages than we were expecting. It is still concerned about enterprise and executive salarly deals but that was not to the fore here. We expect the economic data over the next month will be weak enough to make the market look for another cut, but since the easing was so linked to inflation we may have to wait until the February board meeting when the bank will have Q4 CPI data."
